name: field keys: the keyboard as a MIDI source

pr.title: Add field keys: the computer keyboard as a MIDI source, with keymaps (keyboard-instrument.md chunk 1)
pr.head: cd3a125d07e269eb6c5d780efc6fad5e83c9c2f5

summary: Field makes sound by rendering files offline, and until now nothing in it took notes. This pull request adds field keys, which turns the computer keyboard into a MIDI instrument. It publishes a virtual MIDI source named Field Keys, so Logic or any other application that lists MIDI inputs can play from it. It is chunk 1 of the keyboard-instrument plan. Later chunks play a SuperCollider instrument from the same source and record what you play.

Three problems shape the design. A terminal normally reports only key presses, and a note needs its release, so field keys turns on the kitty keyboard protocol and refuses a terminal that lacks it. Keyboard layouts move characters around, so it reads the physical position of each key rather than the character it types. And what each key plays should be yours to change, so it comes from a keymap: a YAML file, checked by a zod schema, that reloads when you save it.
A key press travels through four steps:

1. The terminal reports the key. decodeTerminal turns the protocol's escape sequences into key events, each a press, a repeat, or a release.
  2. The event gets a position. PressedKeys resolves a press to a position such as KeyA, and makes the release reuse it.
  3. The session decides the MIDI. KeysSession looks the position up in the keymap and returns note-ons, note-offs, controller changes, or pitch bend.
  4. The helper sends it. Each message goes as one NDJSON line to field-audiod --keys, which sends it from Field Keys.

The native work is two short-lived modes of the existing field-audiod binary rather than an npm MIDI module, so the TypeScript side gains no native dependency. Everything about notes and keymaps is TypeScript that vitest covers without the native build.

cards.title: Terms on this page
cards.html:
• Position. A physical key, named by its W3C KeyboardEvent.code value, such as KeyA. The name comes from the US key in that place, but it means the place.
  • Keyboard layout. The operating system's map from position to character: QWERTY, Dvorak, AZERTY.
  • Keymap. Field's map from position to what the key plays: a note, a chord, or a control.
  • Kitty keyboard protocol. A terminal protocol that reports press, repeat, and release as escape sequences, for a program that asks.
  • Base layout key. The protocol's optional field naming the US key at the same place as the key pressed.
  • Helper. field-audiod --keys, the native process that owns the virtual source and reports the keyboard layout.
  • Dead key. A key that types nothing alone and waits to combine with the next key.

groups.title: The keymap format
groups.kicker: The YAML schema every keymap passes, and the built-in Musical Typing keymap
intro: A keymap says what each physical key plays. It names keys by position: the W3C KeyboardEvent.code value, such as KeyA or Semicolon. The name comes from the key a US keyboard has in that place, but it means the place, whatever your layout types there. A keymap binds each position to a note, written as an offset in semitones from base, or to a control: transpose, velocity, pitch bend, a MIDI controller, or panic.

keymapSchema checks every keymap, built-in or yours, and each error names the position and the rule it breaks. A grid assigns offsets to whole rows by a rule, so an isomorphic keymap takes one line. The schema also expands the grid, because the range rule needs the expanded notes. The rules:

• Known positions only. The four named rows, Backquote, Backslash, IntlBackslash, Space, Tab, and the arrows.
  • A note or a control, never both.
  • Escape is reserved, so no keymap can stop you quitting.
  • Every note is in MIDI's 0 to 127 range at base, and the keymap plays at least one note.

files.note: The schema, the bindable positions, grid expansion, and toKeymap, which turns a parsed file into the maps the session reads.

checks.text: The fourths fixture expands to 48 on KeyZ, 53 on KeyA, 58 on KeyQ, and 63 on Digit1, as plan §2.4 says. src/schema/keymap.test.ts asserts it, and its 13 cases pass at this head.
Named rows now count toward the "appears twice" rule, so rows: [home, home] and rows: [home, [KeyA]] are both rejected. A schema test covers both, and it passes at this head.

files.note: The default keymap, after Logic Pro's Musical Typing: C4 on KeyA, black keys on the row above, transpose and velocity on KeyZ to KeyV, sustain on Tab while held, and pitch bend and modulation on the number row.

groups.title: Reading key events from the terminal
groups.kicker: The kitty keyboard protocol: probe, enable, decode, and restore
intro: A terminal normally sends only the text a key types, and repeats a held key. The kitty keyboard protocol lets a program ask for press, repeat, and release events, sent as escape sequences. Ghostty, iTerm2 3.5 and later, kitty, and WezTerm implement it. Apple's Terminal does not.
src/keys/terminal.ts holds the byte-level half:

• The probe. probeKittyProtocol asks for the protocol's flags and then for the device attributes, which every terminal answers. A terminal with the protocol answers the first question before the second.
  • Enable and restore. ENABLE pushes flags 1, 2, 4, and 8 and turns on focus reports, so a lost focus can release every held note. RESTORE undoes both.
  • The decoder. decodeTerminal is a pure function from bytes to events. It carries a sequence cut off at the end of one chunk over to the next.
  • Quitting. isQuit says which events quit: Esc and Ctrl-C. On a layout with no c, such as Russian, Ctrl-C is the key at the US c position.

files.note: The protocol strings, the decoder, the quit rule, and the probe.

checks.text: Ctrl-C is the key that types c, or, when the typed key is outside ASCII, the key whose base layout key is c. So under Russian, CSI 1089::99;5u quits, and under Dvorak the key at the US c position, which types j, does not. terminal.test.ts covers both, and both pass at this head.
The probe drops complete key events and returns only a cut-off tail as rest, as this comment says. A test feeds CSI 97u, both answers, CSI 115u, and a cut-off CSI 1, and gets rest: "\x1b[1".

groups.title: Finding the physical key
groups.kicker: Turning a key event into a position, from the base layout key or the keyboard layout
intro: The protocol reports the character a key types under the current keyboard layout. On Dvorak the key at KeyS types o, so reading characters would scatter Musical Typing across the keyboard. positionOf recovers the position from these sources, in order:

1. The base layout key. A terminal can add the US key at the same place. Ghostty sends it, but the protocol lets a terminal leave it out when it equals the typed key.
  2. The keyboard layout report. On macOS the helper reports what each position types under the active layout, and reports again when the input source changes. charactersToPositions inverts each report once.
  3. QWERTY. With neither, a character reads as its own US position.

PressedKeys makes a release take the position its press resolved to. Without it, a release that lacks its press's base layout key, or arrives after an input-source switch, could resolve to another position and leave a note sounding. Plan §9.1 records that a run under a ColemakC layout showed this.

A dead key types nothing alone and waits for the next key, so the terminal may never report it. unplayablePositions names the bound positions that are dead keys under the current layout, for the status line.

files.note: Position lookup, the press-to-release memory, and dead-key reporting.

groups.title: The note state
groups.kicker: KeysSession turns positions into MIDI and pairs every note-on with one note-off
intro: KeysSession holds everything between a position and MIDI bytes: transpose, velocity, which position holds which notes, held controllers, and toggles. It returns MIDI messages as byte arrays and sends nothing itself, which lets vitest cover it without a helper. It keeps four promises:

• Every note-on gets exactly one note-off. Two keys can sound one note, through a shared chord note or a transpose, so holders counts the keys that hold each note. The first press sends the note-on and the last release sends the note-off.
  • A release ends what its own press started. held remembers the notes and channel of each press, so a transpose or a reloaded keymap in between does not change what the release turns off.
  • Modifiers block presses, never releases. A press with Ctrl, Alt, Cmd, Hyper, or Meta does nothing. Shift and the lock bits change nothing. A release always ends its notes.
  • Focus-out and quit release everything. releaseAll sends a note-off for each held note and resets held controllers. quit adds All Notes Off (CC 123).
  • A toggled controller does not outlive its keymap. Quit, panic, and a reload send 0 for each controller a toggle key left on, so a toggled sustain cannot hold the receiver's notes after field keys has gone.

files.note: The session state machine and the MIDI byte encoders.

checks.text: Its 21 tests pass at this head. They include a shared note released in either order, a transpose while a key is held, a release that carries Ctrl, the transpose bounds, and toggled controllers turned off at quit, panic, and reload.
setKeymap now returns these messages, and play sends them, so each save that passes validation turns a toggled sustain off. That releases any notes the pedal was holding.

groups.title: Choosing, loading, reloading, and printing keymaps
groups.kicker: Where a keymap comes from, how a saved edit reaches the session, and --print
intro: resolveKeymapSource applies the rule Field already uses for instrument programs. A bare name only ever names a built-in in keymaps/. A value with a /, or ending in .yaml, is a path, and a leading ~/ means your home directory. --keymap wins over FIELD_KEYMAP, which wins over musical-typing. There is no search path, so your file can never shadow a built-in.

watchKeymap watches the directory that holds the keymap, not the file. Many editors save by renaming a temporary file over the original, and a watch on the file would keep following the old one. It reloads only when the text changed. A saved file that fails validation leaves the current keymap in place, and its first error shows in the status line.
printKeymap draws a keymap as a keyboard, with the note or control in each key's place, for field keys --print. Notes use scientific pitch notation, where MIDI note 60 is C4.

files.note: Resolving a name or path, loading and validating, and the reload watch.
The --print diagram and the control descriptions.

checks.text: Running field keys --print at this head drew the Musical Typing diagram, with C4 on A and T-12 and T+12 on Z and X, and exited 0.

groups.title: The native helper
groups.kicker: Two short-lived field-audiod modes: --keys owns the source and reports the layout, --midi-monitor prints a source
intro: field-audiod is Field's native daemon, written in C++ with JUCE. This pull request adds two modes that run as their own short-lived processes, apart from the shared daemon, so they never touch its transport or socket:

• --keys <name>. Reports the keyboard layout, creates the virtual source with JUCE's MidiOutput::createNewDevice, and prints a ready line. Then it sends each {"midi":[...]} line from stdin as it arrives. At the end of its input it closes the source and exits 0, so Field Keys disappears with field keys. A malformed line gets an error line and exit 1.
  • --midi-monitor <name>. Opens a named MIDI source and prints each message as NDJSON until end of input, SIGTERM, or SIGINT. The round-trip test and a person checking a controller both use it.

keyboard-layout.cpp reads the active layout through the macOS Text Input Sources API. For each bindable position it asks UCKeyTranslate what that key types with no modifiers, and it marks dead keys. A distributed notification reports input-source switches. The file includes no JUCE headers, and on Linux it reports nothing.

files.note: Both modes: the NDJSON reader that sends MIDI, the layout report, and the monitor.

checks.text: A field-audiod built from this head passed all 8 round-trip cases in src/keys/helper-native.test.ts on macOS, and the new C++ files added no compiler warnings.

files.note: The macOS layout reader and the input-source watcher.
Parses --keys and --midi-monitor and returns before any socket or audio device exists.
Adds the two sources and links Carbon on macOS for the Text Input Sources API.

groups.title: Talking to the helper
groups.kicker: KeysHelper spawns field-audiod --keys and speaks its NDJSON, tested with a stub and with the real binary
intro: KeysHelper spawns field-audiod --keys, found the way the daemon is found: daemonBinary(), or FIELD_AUDIOD. It resolves once the helper prints its ready line, passes each keyboard layout report to its caller, and reports an exit after ready with the helper's last error. Closing the helper's stdin is how field keys removes the source.

Two test files cover it. helper.test.ts runs against a Node stub, so it needs no native build. helper-native.test.ts runs the real --keys and --midi-monitor together and checks that notes arrive in order. On a Linux machine without the ALSA sequencer, each case skips by name and says why, so a green run without a MIDI service never reads as coverage.

files.note: Spawning the helper, parsing its lines with zod, and closing it.

checks.text: The start promise rejects on the exit event, which Node can emit before the child's stdout is read. 300 starts of a stub that printed an error line and exited at once all rejected with the stub's message, so the error line was never lost.
The expected positions come from TEXT_POSITIONS in the schema. So a position added there fails this test until keyboard-layout.cpp reports it.

files.note: A comment only: it records that the native round trip skips by name on the Linux runner.

checks.text: CI's Linux job passed at this head, and its log shows each native case skipping by name because /dev/snd/seq is missing.

groups.title: The field keys command
groups.kicker: Wires the terminal, positions, session, helper, and reload together, and gives the terminal back on every exit
intro: keysCommand loads the keymap first, so --print and a broken keymap exit before the command touches the terminal. Then withKittyKeyboard puts the terminal in raw mode, probes for the protocol, and enables it. It undoes all three on a return, a throw, or a process exit.

play starts the helper, starts the reload watch for a keymap given by path, and handles stdin. A quit event stops. A focus-out releases everything and forgets remembered positions. Each key event goes through PressedKeys and the session to the helper. On stop, play sends the quit sequence and closes the helper. One status line shows the keymap, transpose, velocity, sounding notes, dead-key positions, and any reload error.

files.note: The interactive shell: terminal setup and restore, the event loop, and the status line.

groups.title: Docs and the plan
groups.kicker: docs/keys.md as the reference, links to it, and the plan marked in progress
intro: docs/keys.md is the reference for players and keymap writers: the supported terminals, playing, how positions work, the default keymap, choosing a keymap, and the keymap format. README.md, docs/README.md, and AGENTS.md link it, and docs/architecture.md describes the two new daemon modes.

The plan moves from ready to in-progress. Its new §9 records what implementation settled, such as a release taking its press's position and the two-second probe wait. It also records what was verified and how, and what is still owed: criteria 1 to 20 by hand at a real keyboard, Linux, and a one-off CoreMIDI failure. Every open question in §7 is deferred to a later chunk.

files.note: The new user reference for field keys and the keymap format.

checks.text: The monitor command now gives the path the build writes, run from the Field checkout, and the text above it says why field-audiod is not on your PATH. Plan criterion 1 uses the same path.

A reload sends 0 for each controller a toggle key left on, through setKeymap, which play calls only after a save that validates. So this sentence holds, and a save that fails validation leaves a toggle on. The Actions table says the same for quit and panic, as quit and the panic action do.
